subject: Civil Engineering
title: Landslides: When Slopes Fail
description: A micro-lesson that makes Landslides: When Slopes Fail usable.

hook.text: In 2014, a hillside near Oso, Washington slid across a valley — 43 people died.

buildup.text: Slopes fail when the driving forces — gravity and water — exceed resisting forces.

discovery.text: The factor of safety is the ratio of resisting forces to driving forces. Below 1.0, it slides.

twist.text: Heavy rainfall is the top trigger. Water adds weight and reduces soil friction.

climax.text: Slope stability analysis is required before any hillside construction project.

punchline.text: Gravity never forgets. Water always helps it remember.

quiz.question: What is the primary trigger for most landslides?
options: Heavy rainfall adding weight and reducing soil friction
Trees falling and destabilizing the surface

details.summary: Landslides occur when the driving forces on a slope, primarily gravity acting on the soil mass, exceed the resisting forces from soil shear strength along a potential failure surface.
details.whyItMatters: Landslides cause billions of dollars in damage and thousands of deaths annually worldwide. Understanding slope stability is essential for safe construction on or near hillsides and for protecting existing communities.
takeaways: Landslides occur when driving forces exceed restraining forces on a slope
Water infiltration is the most common landslide trigger because it reduces strength
Factor of safety is the ratio of resisting forces to driving forces along a slip surface

faq.question: Why does rainfall trigger so many landslides?
faq.answer: Rainfall infiltrates into slope soil, raising pore water pressure, which reduces effective stress and therefore shear strength along potential failure surfaces. Simultaneously, the added water weight increases the driving force on the slope.

faq.question: How do engineers analyze slope stability?
faq.answer: Engineers calculate the factor of safety for the most critical potential failure surface by comparing the sum of resisting forces (soil strength along the surface) to driving forces (gravity component of soil weight).
